Sources indicate that “Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”.

A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

But if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

But that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

By our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

The fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

Recent findings suggest that the next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In Newly introduced York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

Sources indicate that “Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”.

In a recent development, “The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”.

According to recent reports, peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”.

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

Sources indicate that martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I stated, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”.

In a recent development, with Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

It has been revealed that “He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:.

According to recent reports, “There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ stated Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” states Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”.

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

According to recent reports, “Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

Industry observers note that “Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

“Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

#24649. The world’s most precious brain samples — and what they teach us about being human

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2183 w)
📖 Baca

The world’s most precious brain samples — and what they teach us about being human

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A neuron from the human hippocampus.
  • Neuroscientist Lucy Palmer and her team have been waiting days for this moment.
  • Landmark map of human brain’s gene activity holds clues to Alzheimer’s disease and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A neuron from the human hippocampus. The bushy branches receive signals from other neurons. Credit: Jake Watson and Rebecca Morse-Mora, Jonas group, ISTA.

Neuroscientist Lucy Palmer and her team have been waiting days for this moment.

Landmark map of human brain’s gene activity holds clues to Alzheimer’s disease and more.

Landmark map of human brain’s gene activity holds clues to Alzheimer’s disease and more.

Across the road from her laboratory, at the Royal Melbourne Hospital in Australia, surgeons are removing brain tissue from a person with brain cancer. They set some aside for Palmer to collect and study. It is about the size of a shelled peanut.

A colleague of hers takes the sample, places it in a tub of artificial cerebrospinal fluid and rushes it back to the lab, securing it in a chamber filled with bubbling carbon dioxide and oxygen to keep it alive.

These precious samples can survive for only a day or so before they start to deteriorate, so Palmer’s team wastes no time. Within half an hour of receiving the tissue, they are recording the electrical current passing between neurons as they fire.

According to recent reports, palmer’s group at the Florey Institute in Melbourne is using live brain tissue to understand more about brain cancers and how the activity of neurons influences tumour growth. Her lab, and others using such samples, are doing something rare — measuring how live, working human neurons behave.

Sources indicate that most studies of brain-cell function rely on tissue taken from people who have died or from living animals. Post-mortem human brains, however, preserve only the structure and not the activity of cells, and the brains of other animals might function differently. “As much as we like mice, I don’t want to understand the mouse brain. I want to understand the human brain,” Palmer indicates.

Recent findings suggest that slices from a sample of living human brain ready for study.Credit: Emmalyn P. Leonard.

Working with living brain tissue from another person is both humbling and a great privilege, she says. “Every sample is precious.” It’s also an artisanal skill: attaching recording equipment to individual neurons requires the neuroscientific equivalent of a gardener’s green fingers. It relies on mastery of a decades-old technique called patch-clamping, which has fallen out of fashion as flashier recording methods have become available.

Despite the barriers, there is increasing interest in this rare resource. The number of studies published about this tissue has increased from just a handful two decades ago to upwards of 40 a year, according to data from Scopus, with the bulk attributed to about ten research teams. Neuroscientists around the world are working with surgeons to access the tissue and keep it alive in their labs for periods of time ranging from 24 hours to a few weeks, investigating the intrinsic electrical properties of cells and how they communicate with each other during both health and disease.

“When looking into a disease, being able to look directly at the human tissue is absolutely vital,” says Palmer.

Neuroscientists have many ways to study the human brain: non-invasive scanning, indirect measures such as blood samples and, after death, in slices under the microscope. They can also study brain function directly in animal models and, very rarely, in people who have electrodes implanted while they are undergoing surgery. But none of those approaches allows scientists to measure and manipulate the activity of individual human brain cells in their natural environment.

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture.

How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture.

That has changed in the past ten years, says Scott Owen, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California. Although people have been studying live human tissue since the 1970s, he says, the field has finally reached a point at which enough is known about the mammalian brain to understand how human brains differ from those of other animals.

Recent findings suggest that his team works with paediatric neurosurgeons to acquire tissue taken from children with epilepsy, cancer or abnormal tangles of blood vessels in their brains. By comparing samples from people with different diseases, the researchers can look for features common to all donors and deduce which are conserved properties of the human brain, rather than artefacts of any one condition.

In a preprint published in September, for instance, Owen and his colleagues found distinct differences in how human pyramidal neurons — significant, bushy brain cells that live in the cortex — mature compared with those of mice1. The team analysed neocortex samples from 24 children and teenagers, ranging in age from 9 months to 18 years, and mouse samples from equivalent developmental stages. The study, which is yet to be peer reviewed, looked at patterns in how neurons fire, or spike. It’s known that human neurons are quicker to spike after a stimulus than are rodent neurons and that this might correlate with intelligence. Owen and his colleagues found that human neurons got faster at responding over the course of development, with neurons from teens spiking more rapidly than those from children; the opposite happened in mice.

Slices from a sample of living human brain, ready for study.Credit: Rennie Kendrick.

Recent findings suggest that when the researchers looked at the genes that might explain how this happens, they found two that increased in expression over time in people, but not in mice. These genes help to create ion channels in cell membranes, which allows signals to travel between neurons. Faults in these genes have been linked to several neurodevelopmental conditions2.

According to recent reports, karri Lämsä, a biophysicist at the Hungarian Centre of Excellence for Molecular Medicine in Szeged, is also interested in how human neurons fire and how these patterns might change with time and newly introduced experiences. His team studies centimetre-wide cubes of the cortex that are discarded during surgeries to enable access to deeper parts of the brain. In a study published last year, they looked at a type of neuron that inhibits others. In these cells, the axon — the main trunk — transmits signals faster and spikes at lower thresholds than in the same cells in mice3. Fast-acting neurons of this type are thought to have a crucial role in complex brain functions.

It has been revealed that lämsä’s team has also been studying how networks of these fast-spiking neurons might change with age. In samples taken from 106 people ranging in age from 11 to 84 years, the researchers found that these circuits become weaker over time and the spikes in electricity travelling across the cell membrane become smaller and slower4. These changes could explain why the human brain becomes less capable of learning and processing information as people age.

According to recent reports, other work using live human tissue has challenged a key assumption about the human brain: that it is a scaled-up version of the mouse brain. Peter Jonas, a neuroscientist at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria in Klosterneuburg, is using live human tissue to understand how brain cells function alone and in networks. Jonas had worked with animal models for more than 30 years when, in 2022, he began collaborating with a neurosurgeon at the Medical University of Vienna. He would receive tiny samples of human brain tissue — mainly from the hippocampus — measuring about one-fifth of a teaspoon.

It has been revealed that can your brain grow upcoming neurons? How researchers are solving a century-old puzzle.

Can your brain grow upcoming neurons? How researchers are solving a century-old puzzle.

Sources indicate that his lab’s work suggests that some properties of the human brain, such as the number of dendritic spines (tiny outgrowths at the end of synapses that connect neurons), follow different scaling rules from those of the mouse. Neurons are also more densely connected in the human neocortex — the area of the brain thought to control higher functions such as decision-making and planning — than in the mouse one, but have fewer connections in the hippocampus. Jonas says that this kind of information can be gleaned only from living tissue.

In a 2025 Cell study examining tissue taken from the hippocampus and cortex, his team also found that the electrical signals transmitted between neurons were more reliable and precise than they were in mouse brains5. The synapses in human brains successfully triggered the receiving cell to fire 90% of the time, compared with a 62% success rate in mice. Computer modelling by Jonas’s team suggests that reliable transmission could set the human brain apart from those of other species. “We are at the beginning of understanding this,” claims Jonas.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Palmer has observed that the excitability of brain cells differs between humans and rodents6, which could be because human dendrites are twice as wide as those of mice. Differences in size also affect how the cells handle information, she says. Larger neurons with longer, bushier branches can form widespread networks, whereas smaller neurons restrict a network to their close neighbours.

Recent findings suggest that palmer also finds human tissue invaluable for studying disease. Cancers in mouse brains are generally composed of a limited number of cell types, whereas every single cell in a human brain tumour is different. Furthermore, most brain cancer research in mice has focused on one particular type of cancer, called glioblastoma.

Recent findings suggest that neurons from the human cortex next to their neighbours. Scientists can record from several branches of these complex neurons to monitor their activity.Credit: Jake Watson, Jonas group, ISTA.

Using slices of human brain tissue, Palmer and her team have found that cancer cells taken from aggressive tumours were more active than those in slower growing tumours7, boosting signalling and forming more synapses with neurons. The researchers also found that neurons were generally more active in people with aggressive tumours and that this increased activity leads to greater spread of cancer cells, confirming results from animal models.

Recent findings suggest that in a study testing the efficacy of a drug for brain cancer, Palmer’s team also saw changes to excitability and signalling in neurons8. Together, the findings could explain how the drug slows down tumour growth, or halts it entirely.

One of the biggest challenges of working with living human brain tissue is a specialist technique that scientists need to learn. Called patch-clamping, the technique involves pressing the tip of a glass micropipette against the membrane surrounding a neuron and using suction to make a tight seal. A cell’s electrical activity can then be measured through one or several ion channels in the membrane. These measurements are used to study how a neuron behaves in response to different stimuli.

In a recent development, patch-clamping was invented in the 1970s and is an indispensable tool in electrophysiology. It stands in stark contrast to techniques such as calcium imaging and optical imaging, which allow scientists to measure electrical activity in thousands of neurons at once. These techniques are more expensive but less technically challenging, states Palmer. In comparison, “patch-clamping takes a year to learn and years to understand,” she says. “You never master it.”.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt is set to inspect documentation in person regarding Fifa’s deeply contentious World Cup private investment proposal, it is understood.

The global governing body dispatched a letter on 2 November to members of the Fifa Council – where Hewitt serves as a Fifa vice-president – offering them the opportunity to examine the files at its headquarters in Zurich.

Sources indicate that hewitt is believed to have taken up the offer, though a firm date for the trip remains unconfirmed. Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin is likewise thought to have agreed to attend.

Relations between Uefa and Fifa president Gianni Infantino broke down over the project, which involved creating a new entity named Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) to manage commercial and operational activities for both the men’s and women’s World Cups alongside other Fifa tournaments.

Under the blueprint, a minority shareholding in FFE was to be acquired by private investors, led by Thrive Capital, an entity established by Joshua Kushner, whose brother is the son-in-law of United States President Donald Trump.

The initiative was ultimately scrapped following opposition from Uefa and a pair of other continental confederations.

Hewitt’s career experience in private equity provides her with direct insight into the standard documentation and financial details expected in proposals of this nature.

Fifa issued the invitation after European representatives on the Fifa Council sent a formal letter on 19 October requesting clarity on several matters, including the FFE arrangement and disciplinary proceedings involving Folarin Balogun.

Provisions regarding non-disclosure agreements and the specific terms governing document inspection in Zurich have yet to be finalised.

The FA offered no comment on the matter.

Earlier on Tuesday, the French Football Federation formally endorsed Philippe Diallo’s bid for the Fifa presidency.

On Monday, Uefa confirmed that the 63-year-old had secured the support of national association delegates across its executive committee and the Fifa Council to challenge Infantino.

Disquiet over the FFE proposals prompted European football’s governing body to promise in August that it would put forward a credible challenger to Infantino.

Industry observers note that diallo’s domestic federation has now unanimously backed his campaign, stating: "World football is going through a pivotal period in its history. The challenges affecting its governance demand clear thinking and responsibility.

"Restoring trust, preserving the universality of football, rebuilding Fifa’s credibility, and placing the development of football in all regions of the world at the heart of its actions are essential complications for the entire international football community.

"By accepting this invitation, Philippe Diallo is responding to a desire to open a newly introduced chapter for the governance of world football.".

Figures within Uefa had previously hoped that former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, who presently serves as Fifa’s chief of global football development, might enter the race, though he is believed to have declined the prospect last week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.

The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner revealed after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia noted a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy.".

Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.

"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

It has been revealed that pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing.".

A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia stated at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.

Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

Sources indicate that "Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases.".

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska noted.

Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist states.

According to recent reports, ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on latest US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia.".

Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Recent findings suggest that kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov stated the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.

"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov mentioned.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.

In a recent development, "Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Sources indicate that iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy mentioned he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.

Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

According to recent reports, pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the matter is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meet the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contenders.

Voting for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026 has now closed.

Fans worldwide have been voting from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be revealed as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - were nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covered the period September 2025-August 2026.

Read more on the five contenders.

Listen: Who is your BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026?

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Temwa Chawinga.

Club: Kansas City Position: Forward.

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Ewa Pajor.

Club: Barcelona Position: Forward.

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland and is the team's leading goalscorer.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alexia Putellas.

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder.

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3â0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alessia Russo.

Club: Arsenal Position: Forward.

Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.

She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.

Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.

It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.

Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.

She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Khadija Shaw.

Club: Manchester City Position: Forward.

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a fresh four-year contract through to 2030.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.
  • Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim.
  • Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

Sources indicate that “Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he noted, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”.

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg remarked Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice.

According to recent reports, ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he stated on Facebook.

According to recent reports, the state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Sources indicate that not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

In a recent development, at the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and mentioned he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last.

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and noted at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”.

It has been revealed that for the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he stated in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Ipswich Town boss David Wright praised the football intelligence of Wales international Mary McAteer following her first goal for the club.
  • McAteer joined Town on loan from Charlton Athletic in September as part of a revamp of the squad following last season's ninth-place finish in Women's Super League 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mary McAteer celebrates after scoring Ipswich's opening goal at Watford.

Ipswich Town boss David Wright praised the football intelligence of Wales international Mary McAteer following her first goal for the club.

McAteer joined Town on loan from Charlton Athletic in September as part of a revamp of the squad following last season's ninth-place finish in Women's Super League 2.

She headed home the rebound after skipper Maria Boswell's fierce shot came back off the crossbar against Watford and they went on to win Sunday's game 2-1.

The victory put Town third - and in the play-off places - in only their second season at that level.

"Every time Bos gets the ball in that area now, in my head I'm thinking, 'just shoot'," Wright told BBC Radio Suffolk.

"Mary is a really intelligent footballer - she uses her intelligence to find space between the lines, it allows her link through the thirds, and it's another sign of her intelligence that when Bos hits a beautiful strike, it hits the bar, bounces down, she's the first one to react and nods it in.".

Ipswich on 'inevitable' path to WSL - Boswell.

Kit Graham added Ipswich's second as they bounced back positively from a 2-1 home league defeat by Bristol City and midweek loss to McAteer's parent club Charlton in the Players' Cup.

"It has been a really tough week, not just physically, but also psychologically - three different challenges," noted Wright.

"What good teams do is they bounce back. To finish the week off, going to Watford and coming away with three points, the girls should be really proud of themselves.".

Boswell said last month that she believes it is "inevitable" that Town will eventually achieve their goal of a place in the top flight of English women's football.

But despite their current position, Wright insisted it was not a focus for him.

"I don't really look at the table. I want to push them, make them better and if we do that we will keep moving in the right direction - that process is getting better every day and will help us achieve what we want to achieve," he said.

Wright's side have won five of their eight WSL 2 games but now have over a month to wait before the next, when they travel to bottom-of-the-table Durham.

"I was looking at the calendar on the wall and I've never known such a major gap. The good thing is we've got lots of games in between so we'll be busy and when the Durham game comes round, the girls will be ready," Wright added.

Teenage wonderkid JJ Gabriel has appeared to confirm his Manchester United exit in a video posted on social media.

The 16-year-old, who has never played a competitive match for the first team, joined United as a 10-year-old in 2020.

He has been absent from the club since requesting in September that his registration be cancelled, shortly before his 16th birthday on 6 October.

Gabriel made no mention of where he intends to go next, but widespread speculation has linked him with Real Madrid, and his goodbye video on Instagram appears to have edged him closer to a move to the Spanish giants.

Industry observers note that gabriel noted in his video: “Dear Manchester United, I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with massive dreams. Here I grew as a player and a person. From scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy Award.

“You gave me moments I will always treasure. To every coach and every member of staff, to my team-mates and everyone who supported me, thank you for believing in me and helping me grow.

Sources indicate that “As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be a part of my story. Thank you for everything, JJ.”.

The teenager is the son of former Republic of Ireland international Joe O’Cearuill.

Last season he became the youngest ever winner of United’s Jimmy Murphy Award, given to the club’s young player of the year.

Despite his absence, Gabriel had remained registered to United, who the Press Association understands are ready to explore legal options against the youngster’s next club over possible broken regulations.

United had initially hoped to persuade him to stay.

It now appears his hat-trick against Sabah on his Uefa Youth League debut on September 10 will be his final appearance for the club.

Gabriel shone in the 5-0 victory, but his representatives were disappointed he was not registered to play later that day in the Champions League fixture against the champions of Azerbaijan.

He had been due to appear in the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton the following week, but had upped sticks by that point.

Had he featured in that tie, Gabriel would have become the club’s youngest player in a competitive match, having already appeared off the bench for Michael Carrick’s side in an August friendly against Atletico Madrid.

#24635. Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX

Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ET: SpaceX has released the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing.
  • Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the tech giant eyes hourly rolls out by 2030.
  • Industry observers note that spaceX is targeting today (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has released the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the tech giant eyes hourly rolls out by 2030.

Industry observers note that spaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship's 15th flight, which will lift off from the firm's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.

Industry observers note that the 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

Industry observers note that if the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage.

This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms.

According to recent reports, "SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk remarked via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6. "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary.".

In a recent development, half of the system is already proven. With catching and reflying boosters largely established, the next and unprecedented step is catching Ship. This is no easy task. The vehicle, returning from orbital speeds, must survive the heat of reentry, make its way precisely back to the pad put itself in position to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. The full recovery of an orbital launch system would, in the words of SpaceX, be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" and would open the "door to airplane-like cadence.".

A successful catch would allow SpaceX to then work on refurbishing Ship for reflight, the next challenge of full reusability. Musk said in August in a SpaceX earnings call that the company will aim to refly the Super Heavy and Ship early next year.

SpaceX has a lot of experience with rocket reuse, as its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket pioneered the practice. But the firm is eyeing another level of reflight with Starship: It's targeting roughly 10,000 debuts of the megarocket per year by 2030, which works out to more than one launch per hour.

"We're aiming to reach 30+ Starship releases/day in 2030, which is ~10k annualized," Musk posted on X in August.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant has repeated that figure to regulators. In comments filed with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in late October, it mentioned that "SpaceX anticipates conducting 10,000 rolls out per year itself." Meanwhile, the recently signed National Space Transportation Policy aims to boost the U.S.'s capabilities to support more than 1,000 rocket launches per year by 2030.

Musk added that SpaceX's planned Starbase Louisiana site alone could support that many Starship debuts. For context: SpaceX released 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, and that was about half of the global total for orbital flights.

Why is SpaceX targeting this incredible increase in launch cadence? It wants to build satellite megaconstellations that dwarf anything the world has ever seen.

In a recent development, the company's V3 Starlink satellites are too large to fly efficiently on the Falcon 9. Each one of the next-gen spacecraft adds 1 terabit of capacity to SpaceX's broadband network, and the 26 flying on Flight 15 are equivalent to around 10 Falcon 9 launches packed with Starlink V2 Mini satellites, according to SpaceX. And the company wants to put a staggering 100,000 V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. (There are currently about 11,000 current-gen Starlink satellites in orbit, and that's by far the largest satellite network assembled to date.).

Industry observers note that spaceX's Starmind project blows even this figure out of the water. SpaceX wants to launch up to 1 million satellites to serve as orbital AI data centers, and it appears to be making the moves terrestrially regarding the hardware. On Nov. 10, German firm Singulus Technologies announced a contract worth more than 60 million euros for a solar cell production line for Starmind satellites, which SpaceX builds in Bastrop, Texas. Musk remarked the order covers equipment for 100 gigawatts of solar cells per year. In terms of orbital hardware, the project is only feasible if SpaceX can reach its targeted "airplane-like cadence.".

The gap between SpaceX's vision and the situation today is vast. Starship flew four times in 2024 and five times in 2025, and Flight 15 would be its fourth launch of 2026. Musk mentioned on the earnings call that he expects Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half of 2027, and twice weekly or more by the end of that year. Starbase in Texas is presently authorized for 25 rolls out per year, and the Louisiana site is not expected to host a launch before 2029.

In a recent development, even a perfect outing for Flight 15 and two clean catches will leave lots of work to do. SpaceX will then need to demonstrate reflight with Ship, after assessing the impact on its heat shield system. Then comes orbital refueling, which is a necessary step for any Starship trip beyond LEO and a requirement for SpaceX's commitment to NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. It's unclear how many tanker flights and refuelings will be needed to make a lunar mission possible, but, whatever the number, Starship will probably need to be rapidly reusable. Another step is carrying people. SpaceX has tested life support hardware on the ground in a crew cabin for the moon lander version of Starship that it is building for NASA, but no Starship has flown with such a system.

It has been revealed that there are no guarantees for Flight 15. Ship will only be cleared for a return to Starbase and a catch attempt if it meets safety checks after reaching orbit, which itself is an achievement not to be taken for granted. Flight controllers may end up needing to bring Ship down in the Pacific Ocean or divert its reentry into the Gulf late into flight.

Musk told investors last month that success on this flight is "more likely than not." Whatever happens today and on Saturday, the measure of Starship's progress will soon shift from whether SpaceX can catch a Ship to how quickly it can launch one again.

Industry observers note that andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, Upcoming Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

#24633. ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1180 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players.
  • Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.
  • Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players.

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright confirmed her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

In a recent development, “I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”.

Recent findings suggest that for many years, says the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa introduced its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

It has been revealed that “I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” states Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

“Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”.

It has been revealed that up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

According to recent reports, “More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she claims. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

In a recent development, “There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”.

Some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

When Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she notes. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”.

It has been revealed that though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she says. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie claims candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”.

According to recent reports, the other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she states bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

Recent findings suggest that even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data reveals that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an crucial fact.

London City's 'bravery' paying off in top three pursuit

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • London City earn point in thrilling draw against Arsenal.
  • After 10 games in the Women's Super League season, London City Lionesses have shown they are capable of finishing inside the top three.
  • Their narrow 2-1 defeat by Manchester City two weeks ago provided snippets of their potential but a 1-1 draw at the Emirates against an improved Arsenal on Sunday confirmed their credentials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

London City earn point in thrilling draw against Arsenal.

After 10 games in the Women's Super League season, London City Lionesses have shown they are capable of finishing inside the top three.

Their narrow 2-1 defeat by Manchester City two weeks ago provided snippets of their potential but a 1-1 draw at the Emirates against an improved Arsenal on Sunday confirmed their credentials.

Eder Maestre's side sit third in the table - the last qualification spot for next season's Women's Champions League - and are six points above Arsenal.

It is a strong position to be in just shy of the halfway stage having already faced big hitters Arsenal, Manchester City and Manchester United.

Current leaders Chelsea await in December but, for now, London City's progress is moving at a pace that looks set to challenge the usual suspects.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed.

Goodwin's glorious solo strike draws London City Lionesses level.

A sold-out away end helped fill out the 32,000-strong crowd at the Emirates on Sunday as many hoped for an end-to-end encounter.

They were not disappointed as fearless London City showed bravery against an Arsenal side who played with a spark following their 1-1 draw with Barcelona.

The visitors were helped out by Arsenal's wastefulness - the Gunners had 17 shots and only converted one - but London City caused plenty of problems of their own.

Maestre mentioned after their defeat by Manchester City that their opponents highlighted more experience and know-how but against Arsenal, his side matured.

They were under pressure early on and fell a goal down thanks to Frida Maanum's opener but it took just 98 seconds for Izzy Goodwin to equalise for London City.

That killed Arsenal's momentum and when the pressure increased again from the hosts in the second half, goalkeeper and player of the match Mary Earps stepped up to make crucial saves.

"The performance was there. We had the chances to score and get a better result but Arsenal had chances too. The game was very open," remarked Maestre.

"The way we faced and challenged every circumstance in the game reveals we are here, and able to play with that mentality in these major games.

In a recent development, "We came here to take risks. Our energy was good. We were brave and weren't scared about the context or the opponent.

Sources indicate that "We tried to play as if we were at home. I always want to feel that my teams are brave and go for the win.".

That bravery highlighted as Alexia Putellas came close twice with long-range efforts, Goodwin could have been onside when she was played in behind later on.

London City hit the crossbar through substitute Delphine Cascarino and had 14 shots compared to Arsenal's 17, including four inside the box.

Arsenal are still yet to win at home this season in the WSL but this was still an impressive showing from London City, who came to the Emirates to play.

But while they were willing to take risks, they were smarter than they were against Manchester City, choosing when to press aggressively and when to hold off.

"We tried to match the pace of the ball and not expose ourselves as much to the players that Arsenal have," added Maestre.

It has been revealed that "We were trying to mix the moments we were more clinical in our press. We made some adjustments at half-time and were much better at recognising those.".

London City are backed by US billionaire Michele Kang and that has made a major difference in the transfer market.

They recruited superstars Alexia Putellas, Mary Earps, Mapi Leon and Kadidiatou Diani in the summer.

Such is their depth that high-flying Spaniard Lucia Corrales, the dangerous Cascarino and England international Freya Godfrey came off the bench.

Those individual talents have made a difference and on Sunday it was goalkeeper Earps who took the plaudits, claiming the player of the match award.

She made crucial saves late on as Arsenal pushed ferociously for a winner, tipping Maanum's effort onto the crossbar and blocking her shot from close range.

Earps had to bide her time for the number one shirt after making the switch from Paris St-Germain this summer but has started the past three WSL games.

"Mary is a very strong character and is much more than the things we see in terms of the performance," mentioned Maestre.

"She has experience, and energy that you can bring to every part in the process and not just the things we see in the matches.

"I think the energy that she brings to the position is massive and has a massive impact. I'm very pleased with her.".

Watching on in the stands was England boss Sarina Wiegman who will have been pleased with the display from goalscorer Goodwin.

The 23-year-old got the better of England captain Leah Williamson when she fooled her with quick feet and fired the ball into the back of the net, making it 1-1.

She is proof that competition for places in the London City starting XI is pushing players on and that their depth is improving each week.

"I think Izzy is becoming a more mature player. She has the inner competition and the signings sometimes push you to bring 100% every time," added Maestre.

"She is committed to keep pushing and, with the performances she is having, why not [earn an England call-up]?

"Izzy is moving forward in the ways she can take advantage and that commitment is the way she is reaching those performances. I'm very proud of her.".

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Justin Devenny’s superb strike saw Northern Ireland football earn promotion to the top flight of the Nations League with a hard-fought 1-1 draw away to closest challengers Hungary football in Budapest.

Barnabas Varga ended Northern Ireland’s proud record of not having conceded in this campaign when he fired the hosts in front after 35 minutes – a goal that also sent Hungary to the top of the group.

But moments after Isaac Price had hit the post for Michael O’Neill’s young side, Devenny smashed the ball into the top left-hand corner in the 65th minute to restore Northern Ireland’s one-point advantage as group leaders.

The visitors were on the back foot for much of the first half, with Hungary captain Dominik Szoboszlai hitting the post, but Michael O’Neill, serving a touchline ban in the stands as former captain Steven Davis led things from the touchline, orchestrated key substitutions.

Northern Ireland started with Patrick Kelly in place of the suspended Jamie Donley up front but brought on Josh Magennis at half-time before Kieran Morrison and Brodie Spencer soon followed to help the visitors become a much greater threat going forward.

Magennis’ physical presence and the extra pace paid dividends as, just two years after earning promotion from League C, Northern Ireland completed an unbeaten campaign in Group B2 to secure their place at the top table of European football.

Latest Update: Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers.
  • According to recent reports, who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager?
  • Although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers.

According to recent reports, who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S.

Although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling.

Sources indicate that the United States’ interest in Pep Guardiola, and his talks with Italy earlier, have me wondering – what separates club and international management? Could Pep, as successful as he’s been, do well in either? – Joe P.

Industry observers note that international and club management seem to me related but essentially different jobs. It’s one thing to have the players every day and be able to drill them over and over to impose a philosophy; quite another to pick them up for perhaps a dozen training sessions over a calendar year, plus major tournaments. International football is necessarily less sophisticated than club football, more based on individual excellence or heroism. Guardiola, you suspect, would be able to adapt, but it’s not certain. Plus there’s the fact that at major tournaments players are with their manager for a month or more, cooped up in the same hotel with no release. With the more intense coaches, such as Marcelo Bielsa, that seems to become problematic. And it’s notable that at the last World Cup the nations with the big-name managers – England, Brazil, the United States, Germany – fared less well than those who had appointed technocrats from within.

In a recent development, michael Carrick’s firing highlighted the lack of top-class English managers. Why has an Englishman never managed a Premier League club to a title? – Ricky M.

Industry observers note that I think there are two related complications here. Are there any good English coaches? To which the answer appears to be that there are nowhere near as many as there ought to be. The various changes in player development enacted by the elite player performance initiative and the England DNA project have, over the past 10-15 years, led to the development of far more technically proficient English players than there have ever been before, which has been reflected in the uptick in England’s performances at major tournaments. St George’s Park was supposed to be about developing coaches as well as players but, as yet, that seems not to have happened.

That said, it’s probably also the case that it’s very hard for British coaches to be appointed to top Premier League jobs. Say they get their start at a mid-sized Championship club and win promotion; they then have to amend their approach in the Premier League to scrap for points in a relegation battle. If they fail they are written off as not good enough for the top division; if they succeed, they’re seen as not playing the right sort of football for an elite club. It’s happened to Scott Parker … even the likes of Gary O’Neil or Eddie Howe seem somehow not quite right for the elite who, perhaps understandably, prefer to turn to somebody with experience of European competition.

Is there any part of you that feels sympathy for the current Man City players, who will presumably have to play out a “lost season” thanks to actions they had nothing to do with, and which probably happened long before their time at the club? – Jason D.

Recent findings suggest that to an extent, yes, but they’re pretty naïve if they didn’t realise the potential issue they were walking into. I have far more sympathy for those players who played for clubs who were denied success by City’s cheating. It’s not just the teams who finished second in the league, lost to City in cup competitions or missed out on European qualification because of City; it’s those teams, most obviously Arsenal and Aston Villa, whose development was derailed by City taking their best players, offering wages and transfer fees that it turns out they had no business offering.

Sources indicate that italy have gotten some massive results in the Nations League. Are they back? – Nicholas A.

Recent findings suggest that this question, to be fair, was sent in before the 4-1 defeat to Belgium on Sunday. But anyway, beating France at home may be a substantial result, but that and two wins over Turkey seems limited evidence to say they’re back. They have definitely looked sharper under Roberto Mancini than they have probably since winning the Euros under him five years ago, but that’s a long way from being back. Even if they were to win the Euros in 2028, it wouldn’t alter the fact they haven’t qualified for three World Cups in a row. They need to qualify for 2030 and then probably get to at least the quarter-finals before you can start to say they may be back. And even then, Serie A is way off what it was at its peak – and how many of this squad would get in a Spain or England squad? Even being generous, probably no more than four or five.
